INAM5983.name: Designing the American City
INAM5983.description:
Addresses timely trends, issues, and events. Offers students an opportunity to learn about and respond to issues of the day in an immersive, interdisciplinary format. Content and instructors vary by offering. May be repeated nineteen times.
    
    
        Section information text:
        Designing the American City: Civic Aspirations and Urban Form, is an interpretative look at the characteristic patterns of settlement and attitudes towards cities and urban life that are identified with American urbanization. The course seeks to foster a critical understanding of the cultural aspirations, processes, policies, planning and design actions, which have influenced American urbanization, while introducing visual and analytic skills necessary for its interpretation. The course also addresses the idea of American society, as one historian put it, being “a volatile mixture of hopeful good and curable bad.” We will weigh those soaring American aspirations related to liberty, equality, justice, and the desire to perfect the world, against dystopic aspects of American history such as the near total destruction of Indigenous cultures; the horrors of slavery and systemic racism; the conceits of Manifest Destiny and American exceptionalism; the corporate and political restraints on economic parity; and the despoiling of the environment in the name of progress.

Lastly, the course seeks comparisons and contrasts between periods of rapid urban growth in America, and the even more rapid urban growth currently taking place in many regions of the world.  American cities grew largely in emulation off and in contrast to their much older European counterparts. As today many cities globally seek inspiration from and attempt to improve upon the American urban experience.

Offers specialized topics in journalism for the twenty-first century. Topic matter changes each semester. May be repeated up to eight times.
    
    
        Section information text:
        The 2026 midterm elections are a political turning point for the country— and an opportunity to explore the many forces reshaping American society and culture. This course will explore changing American views on climate change, immigration, and international conflict along with new issues like the rise of the “manosphere” and artificial intelligence. The course will explore the role of the changing media in shaping voter perceptions. Students will combine traditional research (polls, readings, expert analysis) with experiential learning in the form of interviews with voters to analyze what the midterms tell us about America.

        Section information text:
        Students will grapple with the changing landscape of sports media and examine what the future might hold. Artificial intelligence, media rights, and consumer habits have contributed to massive changes in the field. And that doesn’t even get into the changing relationship between athletes and their fans. This class will unpack why those changes have occurred, where the industry is going, and how the shifts impact fans and the media in general. A journalism background is not required for this course.

ME5374.name: Optimization Modeling for Engr
ME5374.description:
Offers topics of current interest in mechanical engineering.
    
    
        Section information text:
        This course provides an introduction to optimization modeling in engineering contexts. Topics covered include linear programming, quadratic and convex programs, and mixed-integer and non-convex models. By the end of the course, students will be equipped to transform practical engineering challenges into optimization models, assess their difficulty, solve them using modern software tools, interpret their solutions, and perform appropriate sensitivity and trade-off analyses. Examples will be drawn from all areas of engineering, as well as computer science and business/finance. Students should have taken a course on linear algebra (MATH 2341 or equivalent) to register for this course.

ME5374.name: ST: Robot Design
ME5374.description:
Offers topics of current interest in mechanical engineering.
    
    
        Section information text:
        Presents the design of robots, with special focus on actuators. Introduces the core principles of machine design, motor modeling, modern transmissions, actuator design, and control architectures. Other advanced topics to be explored include design optimization, series elastic actuation, materials selection, underactuated systems, differential mechanisms, and counterbalanced systems. Combines practical hands-on design exercises and mock design reviews for real-world devices to provide students with the tools needed to design their own robotic systems.

MUSC5973.description:
Focuses on various topics related to music. May be repeated twice for a maximum of 12 total semester hours.
    
    
        Section information text:
        students interested in taking this class need to first interview with Professor Jaeggi (s.jaeggi@northeastern.edu). Course participants will gain research experience by conducting a research project and engage in experiential learning as Research Assistants (RAs) in the Jaeggi Lab (i.e., the SoundMind Collaboratory) within the Brain Game Center for Mental Fitness and Well-Being. As part of this experience, together with their graduate student mentor, student RAs will collect and analyze data for a group project, write a report, and present the project to a larger audience. RAs will contribute to various ongoing research projects in the SoundMind Collaboratory: assisting with the organization and implementation of experiments and helping to design, review, and test experiment materials, recruiting and screening participants, collecting, transcribing, and coding data, performing preliminary analyses, and performing literature searches and writing summaries and reports. To reach these goals, student RAs are required to attend weekly meetings/class sessions, complete the assigned readings, work on their final project, and attend their assigned lab hours and fulfill the obligations as assigned by the SoundMind team. IMPORTANT NOTE: Students are expected to attend class sessions and complete 100 lab hours over the course of the semester (typically 10 lab hours per week, in person), as well as all course assignments (totaling ~15 hours/week).

MUSI2973.name: Festivals Fieldwork
MUSI2973.description:
Focuses on various topics related to the music industry. May be repeated twice for up to 12 total semester hours.
    
    
        Section information text:
        "In this fieldwork research course, students will learn how to design ethnographic research projects and implement them at a multi-day immersive music festival. We will learn about participant-observation, interview techniques, research ethics, how to recruit research participants, qualitative data analysis, and sharing study results. Each student will articulate an original project objective, conduct ethnographic research using appropriate methodologies, and prepare a presentation with their results. An additional course fee covers travel during the semester for supervised research at Furnace Fest, a 3-day punk and hardcore festival in Birmingham, AL. No prior fieldwork experience is required."

PSYC4540.description: Surveys key quantitative topics in psychology and behavioral neuroscience. Emphasizes theory and modeling, not statistics. Specific topics vary, but all are drawn from domains in which mathematics and computation play a significant role. Topics may include Fourier analysis with applications to vision and hearing, neural circuit computation, signal detection theory applied to human and nonhuman animals' decisions, measurement of sensory magnitudes in vision and hearing, the linear algebraic theory of color matching in humans, and analysis and models of human response time. Students complete weekly readings and a final project, typically involving use of software for data analysis.

WMNS7900.name: ST: Feminist & Queer Theory
WMNS7900.description:
Examines selected topics in women’s, gender, and sexuality studies. May be repeated up to five times.
    
    
        Section information text:
        This course meets at the GCWS on MIT's campus and on MIT's schedule. Students must apply for acceptance before enrolling in the course. The course is taught by Dr. Heike Schotten (UMass Boston). 
Partly historical and partly topical, this course will introduce you to foundational texts and central questions in each of the respective fields of feminist theory, queer theory, and trans* theory, as well as the difficulties of drawing bright lines between and among these fields. We will explore everything from the Big Questions of field definition down to specific and concrete political phenomena these areas of (sometimes overlapping) feminist, queer, and trans* theory have taken as worthy of attention and interrogation. Assigned readings will privilege the theory part of the course title and pay particular attention to politics.

WMNS7900.name: ST:Women/Gender/Sex S. Asia
WMNS7900.description:
Examines selected topics in women’s, gender, and sexuality studies. May be repeated up to five times.
    
    
        Section information text:
        This course meets at the GCWS on MIT's campus and on MIT's schedule. Students must apply for acceptance before enrolling in the course. This course is taught by Dy. Ayesha Irani (UMass Boston) and Dr. Jyoti Puri (Boston University). 
Women, Gender, and Sexuality in South Asia: Religion, Culture, and Colonial Legacies
This course examines women, gender and sexuality in South Asian history through the lenses of religion, colonialism, and postcolonial culture. Using historical, literary, sociological, and anthropological lenses the course will consider how various institutions of authority—patriarchy, religion, and the state—have shaped and continue to reshape gender and sexuality in South Asia, and how women and other subalterns, in turn, resisted, interpreted and negotiated their position in society. Women and other subalterns continue to be a sign of South Asia’s “backwardness,” but serve simultaneously as a symbolic upon which ideas of modernity are debated. Thus, how women, gender and sexuality are imagined is often at the core of how nation and collective identities are defined and desired in South Asia.
